title: Selective electrochemical CO2 reduction on Cu-Pd heterostructure
abstract: In this work, a novel Cu-Pd heterostructure, derived from CuCl-PdOx hexagonal microplates, was prepared to tune selective single hydrocarbon production from electrochemical CO2 reduction. The CuCl-PdOx hexagonal microplates were synthesized by a dual-potential electrodeposition technique, followed by electrochemical reduction to form Cu-Pd heterostructure. This Cu-Pd heterostructure exhibited a much higher CO2-to-CH4 selectivity (32% Faradaic efficiency, FE) compared to pure Cu or Pd. Moreover, Cu-Pd heterostructure showed excellent suppression on C2H4 generation (below 1% FE) compared to reported Cu nanostructure. The density functional theory calculations suggested that the hollow site of Pd region in the Cu-Pd heterostructure can stablize CO* intermediate and selectively lower the energy demand for CH4 formation rather than C2H4. This work provides new opportunities of designing Cu-based electrocatalysts for selective CO2 reduction to single hydrocarbon.

sections.heading: Research highlights
sections.text: Cu-Pd heterostructure is prepared via dual-potential electrochemical deposition.  The activity and selectivity of CO2 electrochemical reduction is promoted.  Pd in the Cu-Pd can stablize the CO* intermediate and favor CH4 formation.

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
In this work, a novel Cu-Pd heterostructure, derived from CuCl-PdOx hexagonal
microplates, was prepared to tune selective single hydrocarbon production from electrochemical CO2 reduction. The CuCl-PdOx hexagonal microplates were synthesized by a dual-potential electrodeposition technique, followed by electrochemical reduction to form Cu-Pd heterostructure. This Cu-Pd heterostructure exhibited a much higher CO2-to-CH4 selectivity (32% Faradaic efficiency, FE) compared to pure Cu or Pd. Moreover, Cu-Pd heterostructure showed excellent suppression on C2H4 generation (below 1% FE) compared to reported Cu nanostructure. The density functional theory calculations suggested that the hollow site of Pd region in the Cu-Pd heterostructure can stablize CO* intermediate and selectively lower the energy demand for CH4 formation rather than C2H4. This work provides new opportunities of designing Cu-based electrocatalysts for selective CO2 reduction to single hydrocarbon.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
CO2 reduction via electrochemistry is a popular approach to support a sustainable society, because it can utilize renewable electricity to rapidly convert CO2 into valuable chemicals such as HCOOH, CO, CH4, and C2H4 in a mild reaction manner.[1-3] In the past three decades, metal-based catalysts have been extensively studied for this reaction and Cu has been recognized as an exceptional candidate because of its unique capability of reducing CO2 to hydrocarbons with decent Faradaic efficiencies (FEs).[4, 5]
It is widely accepted that CO is a key intermediate to the formation of
hydrocarbons, which is moderately adsorbed on Cu, but the further reaction is readily branched to form various products, leading to a poor selectivity.[1, 5-7] Expecially for the hydrocarbon formation in the H-type reactor, which is a typically multi-electron transfer process. Besides, to start this reaction, a very negative potential has to be applied to activate CO2 molecule before reducing it. Such a high reduction potential results in a low energy efficiency and further deteriorates the selectivity, which substantially limits the practical application of electrochemical CO2 reduction.
Designing a more efficient catalyst is thus essential for the success of this

reaction. Recent advances in material science and computation methodology have accelerated the development in the design and experimental and theoretical screening of catalysts. In the past few years, considerable progresses have been achieved in the morphological and/or compositional control of the Cu-based catalysts using different strategies. On one hand, various morphological types of Cu catalysts, such as Cu nanosheet, branched CuO nanoparticles, star decahedron Cu nanoparticles, Cu nanocavities, and porous hollow fibre Cu have been tested.[8-12] On the other hand, Cu-based alloys, such as CuAu and CuAg have also been prepared.[13-16] These catalysts have successfully enhanced their catalytic activities on electrochemical CO2 reduction compared with bulk Cu catalyst. Theoretical computation studies and experiments have also revealed that it is possible to achieve more efficient and selective CO2 reduction by introducing surface engineering and foreign metal elements into catalysts.[17-21] Although selective CH4 or C2H4 formation has been achieved in several studies, a higher selectivity on a single product is still highly needed for practical applications. In addition, to achieve a high selectivity in hydrocarbon and oxygenates production, a further hydrogenation, rather than production of CO, should be promoted.[22]
Despite of the aforementioned efforts, the recent developments in
heterostructured material have inspired us to design a new type of Cu-based catalyst. Heterostructured materials contain two or more different functional units and have shown promising catalytic activities in many applications. Numerous studies have demonstrated that the interface presented in the heterostructure gives rise to a

synergistic effect, which is the origin of their unique properties and is difficult to obtain from a single-component material or alloy.[23-25] Though it was reported that heterostructured Cu-Au, Cu-Sn or Cu-Zn system could have more benefits in CO2 reduction compared to their alloy counterparts, the behavior of heterostructured material in electrochemical CO2 reduction is largely unknown due to the lack of experimental implementation and theoretical studies.[13, 26, 27] Considering the advantages of a heterostructured material over a bimetallic alloy, the introduction of such an idea may offer a new opportunity in designing catalysts for selective electrochemical CO2 reduction.
The synthesis of heterostructures usually involves sophisticated synthetic control
using surfactants and high temperature, which are of high cost and time consuming. Herein, we proposed a facile approach to prepare Cu-Pd heterojunctions from reducing CuCl-PdOx hexagonal microplates, which synthesized by a dual-potential pulsed electrodeposition method. After pre-reduction, as-prepared Cu-Pd heterojunctions exhibited an excellent catalytic selectivity in electrochemical CO2 reduction. By varying the salt precursor ratio, Cu-Pd with different selectivity was readily obtained. Mechanism studies including Tafel analysis and density functional theory (DFT) calculations were conducted to give an insight into the selective catalytic activity of the Cu-Pd heterostructures.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials and preparation
sections.text:
All chemicals were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Co., China, unless
otherwise specified. Carbon papers (1 cm × 1 cm, TGPH 060, Toray Co, Japan) were used as conducting substrate for the electrodeposition. A typical electrodeposition process was conducted in a mixed solution containing 0.04 M Cu(NO3)2, 0.1 M NaCl, and 0.68 mM Na2PdCl4 (Aladdin Inc., China). A Platinum wire was applied as the counter electrode and a KCl-saturated Ag/AgCl electrode was used as the reference electrode.
To synthesize the CuCl-PdOx microplate precursor, dual-potential pulsed
electrodeposition was applied. A typical potential pulse cycle contained +0.02 V 0.2 s and +0.2 V 0.02 s, successively. After 150 cycles, the electrodeposition was completed. The prepared CuCl-PdOx electrode was rinsed with deionized water for three times and dried under N2 atmosphere. After reduced at -1.6 V for 100 s in CO2 reduction condition, Cu-Pd heterojunctions was obtained. In the synthesis experiments, all potential values were recorded in Ag/AgCl (sat. KCl) scale.

sections.text:
Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction was conducted in a customized
two-compartment cell separated by a perfluorinated ion exchange membrane (GEFC-107, Golden Energy Fuel Cell Co., China). The electrolyte used in both anodic and cathodic compartment was 0.1 M KHCO3 (Sinopharm Co., China, 99.99%). A KCl-saturated Ag/AgCl electrode with a Luggin capillary was used as the reference electrode, and a piece of 2 cm × 2 cm Pt foil was used as the counter electrode. Electrochemical CO2 reduction was conducted with a potentiostat (CHI 760D, CH Instrument Co., China) at 15 oC and 1 atm. To remove dissolved O2 in the catholyte, continuous CO2 (purity 99.999%) was applied to purge (25 mL/min) the catholyte with stirring for 1 h prior the electrolysis. Tafel tests and double layer capacity tests were carried out under the same conditions as the CO2 reduction. The ohmic drop (iR drop) compensation was applied throughout the experiments with current interrupt technique.

sections.heading: 3.1. Synthesis and characterization of the hexagonal microplate precursor
sections.text:
The hexagonal microplate precursor was prepared by a dual potential
electrodeposition, in which two potentials dominated the plate morphology and excluded other morphologies separately (Figure S1). After optimizing the deposit cycles (Figure S2), an exclusive and high-density hexagonal microplate structure was achieved, as characterized by SEM imaging (Figure 1a). The microplates with distinct and sharp edges exhibited the thickness of around 80 nm and a side length of about

1.7 μm (Figure 1b). The composition of the as-prepared hexagonal plate was characterized by XRD. As shown in Figure S3, there were three peaks located at 28.5o, 47.4o, and 56.3o, corresponding well to (111), (220), and (311) of CuCl (JPCDS 82-2114), respectively. The other two peaks at 26.48o and 54.50o corresponded to graphite (JPCDS 75-1621), belonging to the carbon paper substrate. TEM image of a single hexagonal plate (Figure S4) showed the enhanced contrast in plate, implying different components. By HRTEM imaging of plates (Figure 1c), well-crystalline CuCl and Pd nanoparticles with a size of about 5 nm were distinct. The HAADF image and the corresponding elemental mappings (Figure 1d) further demonstrated the existence of Pd nanoparticles and some metal oxides on the hexagonal plate. The survey XPS spectrum (Figure S5a) showed that only C, O, Cl, Cu, and Pd elements existed in the as-prepared hexagonal plate. In the high resolution XPS spectrum of Cu 2p3/2 (Figure S5b), two stronger peaks located at 932.2 eV and 935.2 eV belonged to Cu(I) and Cu(II), respectively. Another peak between 928 eV to 947 eV was the satellite peak of Cu(II). The peak at 915.5 eV ascribed to Cu L3VV (Figure S5c) further confirmed the existence of Cu(I). Cl 2p spectrum in Figure S5d showed two peaks at 198.8 eV and 200.4 eV, which were ascribed to Cl 2p3/2 and Cl 2p1/2 of CuCl, respectively, consistent with the HRTEM imaging. On the other hand, mixed valence status of Pd was found in its high resolution XPS spectrum (Figure S5e) with the Pd 3d5/2 spectrum fitted into Pd (335.9 eV), Pd2O (336.9 eV), and PdO (338.1 eV). The above results indicate that we synthesized hexagonal microplates precursor consisting of CuCl, Pd, and Pd oxides by a novel dual potential electrodeposition, which are Jo ur na l P r -p ro of
denoted as CuCl-PdOx hexagonal microplates hereafter. Interestingly, the dual potential electrodeposition could also synthesize more Cu-based hexagonal microplates precursor with many other metal additions (Figure S6), demonstrating a potentially wide-spread strategy to prepare metal-based material with certain morphology.

sections.heading: 3.2. Characteristics of the Cu-Pd heterostructure
sections.text:
Cu-Pd heterostructure was obtained by electrochemical reduction of CuCl-PdOx
hexagonal microplates. After the pre-reduction under a constant potential, the microplate morphology of hexagonal microplate was destroyed and only particles with size lower than 20 nm could be observed (Figure 2a-2c). The average domain size of these particles was 6.65  2.74 nm (Figure S7). Elemental mapping images (Figure 2d) showed that the Cu and Pd elements remained, while the signal of Cl disappeared, which was also confirmed by the high resolution XPS spectra (Figure S8). Besides, Cu and Pd atoms after the pre-reduction presented uniform dispersion (Figure 2d) in their metallic state. More importantly, the XPS peaks of Pd 3d from Cu-Pd heterostructure moved negatively by averagely 0.3 eV than that from CuCl-PdOx hexagonal microplates while the peaks of Cu 2p moved positively, suggesting the electron transfer from Cu to Pd and the existence of the heterostructure.[36, 37] Thus, Cu-Pd heterostructure was obtained by a simple reduction of CuCl-PdOx hexagonal microplates. sections.heading: 3.3. Electrochemical CO2 reduction on heterostructure
sections.text:
To better investigate the influence of Cu-Pd heterostructure on CO2 reduction, a
series of catalysts with different Pd salt concentration were also applied in CO2 reduction, as shown in Figure 3 and S9. The catalyst without Pd addition (denoted as Cu-Pd-c0) showed only a little amount of HCOOH and CH4 production (less than 5%) from CO2 reduction within the potential window from -0.9 V to -1.4 V vs. RHE (reference electrode similarly hereinafter in experimental part), as shown in Figure 3a. The Cu-Pd heterostructures with gradually increased Pd contents (denoted as Cu-Pd-c1 to -c5, respectively) exhibited much better catalytic activities. From Cu-Pd-c1 to -c3, with the increase in Pd content, FEs of both CH4 and HCOOH increased and their onset potentials moved positively. Besides, a small amount of C2H4 (less than 1% FE) started to appear as the Pd precursor concentration was higher than 0.33 mM (Figure 3c and 3d). However, a further increased Pd content led to a decline of the catalytic performance (Figure 3e and 3f). The only Pd addition catalyst (Figure S10) showed production of HCOOH only less than 3% (Figure 3g). Thus, the best catalytic performance was achieved on the Cu-Pd-c3, with FEs of CH4 higher than 30% at -1.2 and -1.25 V (Figure 4d). HCOOH formation was also detected on the Cu-Pd-c3 and Cu-Pd-c4 at more positive potentials, exemplifying 50% at -1.0 V and 64% at -0.9 V, respectively, which decreased to about 13% at more negative potentials. No CO was detected throughout the experiment, which was possibly attributed to the low production of CO under the detection limit of applied GC. In addition, competitive H2 generation showed about 25% FE on the Cu-Pd-c3 at -1.2 V, Jo rn al Pr -p ro of
which increased gradually in a long-term electrolysis, consistent with the decrease in hydrocarbon generation (Figure S11). This result suggests the instability of hydrocarbon active sites on the Cu-Pd, which was highly structure-sensitive. For a more direct comparison with a bulk electrode, data of a copper foil adopted from our previous study are shown in Figure 4h.[38] The bulk copper foil produced CH4, C2H4, and HCOOH, and their FEs and onset potentials were of similar levels to those reported in literature.[1, 39] Again, the Cu-Pd-c3 showed a better selectivity and activity, compared to this bulk electrode.
Although Cu-based materials are recognized as effective catalysts for the CO2
reduction reaction, the poor performance of the electrodeposited CuCl particles indicated that such a Cu-based structure was not active in our work. On the other hand, previous studies have shown that bulk Pd could reduce CO2 to CO, HCOOH, and CH4 with relatively low FEs,[40] and only Pd nanoparticles less than 10 nm could catalyze CO2 to CO or formic effectively.[41, 42] revealing that the structure and size of materials could drastically change their catalytic behaviors.[43, 44] In our work, Pd nanoparticles around 50-100 nm exhibited poor CO2 reduction performance, consistent with previous findings. Compared to the control groups, the Cu-Pd heterostructures presented a tunable and much enhanced activity, as evidenced by the more positive onset potentials of HCOOH and CH4 as well as higher FEs. More importantly, all the Cu-Pd electrodes, especially on Cu-Pd-c3 and -c4, produced almost exclusively CH4 as the hydrocarbon product from CO2 reduction, only a tiny amount of C2H4 was detected. HCOOH was mainly produced at more positive Jo ur na l P r -p
ro of
potentials (particularly for -0.95 V), corresponding to a potential-dependent selectivity variation on Cu-based electrocatalysts.[45,46] The generation of another two-electron-transfer product CO was possibly too little to reach the detection limit and possibly owing to the faster subsequent hydrogenation for CH4 production, which is consistent with the selective CH4 production reports and will be theoretically discussed in the following section.[47,48] Such a selective production, particularly for high CH4/C2H4 ratio, was hard to be achieved on Cu-based materials. The synergistic effect of Cu-Pd heterostructure might be responsible for the activity and selectivity observed on Cu-Pd.
As shown in Figure 3b to 3f, the CO2 reduction performance of the Cu-Pd
changed along with the variation of Pd content in them (Table S1), showing a tunable activity and selectivity by the introduction of Pd. Structurally, the main difference of these samples caused by the increasing Pd content was the amounts of sites of Cu-Pd interface that exposed on the catalyst surface, because their morphologies were similar. The electrochemical active surface area of Cu-Pd estimated by double layer capacity test (Figure S12) suggests that Cu-Pd held a higher electrochemical active surface compared to the Cu and Pd samples, which could be partially responsible for the high activity of Cu-Pd. Thus, the presence of Cu-Pd interface on the surface, which could create a synergistic effect, should be responsible for this result. Previous studies have confirmed the synergistic effect on the heterostructures in several types of catalytic systems.[49, 50] The catalytic “hotspots” of these synergistic effects are considered to be located near the interface because of the direct electronic and Jo ur na l P re -p
ro of
magnetic communication between different components. In the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction on Cu surface, simultaneous production of CH4 and C2H4 is nearly inevitable, although the optimal potentials for these two products are different. This poor selectivity is attributed mainly to the same key intermediate(s) shared by CH4 and C2H4 in their reaction pathways, which has been confirmed by experimental and theoretical calculation results.[6, 40, 51-55] To form C2 product like C2H4, however, it is essential that a C-C coupling reaction occurs. The adsorption strength and reactivity of the related intermediates would then govern the selectivity. Therefore, it is reasonable to deduce that the synergistic effect on the Cu-Pd interface might change the adsorption behavior of the intermediates and make the C2 formation reaction unfavorable, resulting in a higher activity and selectivity toward CH4 production.

sections.heading: 3.4. Mechanism analysis
sections.text:
To elucidate the mechanism for the CO2 reduction to CH4 on the Cu-Pd
heterostructures, partial current density of CH4 (jmethane) as a function of applied potential was plotted (Tafel plot) in Figure 4. The Cu-Pd-c3 exhibited a Tafel slope of 73.4 mV/decade ranging from -0.95 V to -1.05 V. In comparison, the Tafel slope for the Cu-Pd-c0 was 155.2 mV/decade. The reported Tafel slopes on the Cu catalysts ranged from 60 mV/decade to over 170 mV/decade, depending on the morphology, size, and surface pretreatment of the catalysts.[12, 56, 57] A smaller Tafel slope indicates a better reaction kinetics, because the potential needed to overcome the Jo ur
na l P
re -p

reaction barrier is smaller. These results show that the Cu-Pd heterostructures substantially improved the reaction kinetics compared to pure Cu particles.
To further evaluate the selectivity for CO2 reduction to CH4 on the Cu-Pd
heterostructures, DFT calculations were conducted to explore the free energy change (ΔG) in the CO2 reduction process. According to the experimental data that the heterostructure with a Cu/Pd mole ratio of 4.7 exhibits the most efficient selectivity for CO2 reduction to CH4, the unit slab model with 53 Cu and 11 Pd atoms was used to represent the Cu-Pd heterostructure (Figure S13). The favorable adsorption site for the adsorbate on the surface of Cu-Pd heterostructure was determined by CO*, a common and key intermediate in the formation of both CH4 and C2H4.[1, 6] Based on the comparison of the adsorption energy (ΔEad) of CO on the sites of Cu or Pd region, CO* on the hollow site of Pd region is a more stable structure (Figure S14).[58] Moreover, the charge density difference of CO on the hollow site of Pd region reveals that the electron transfers from the Cu-Pd substrate to the adsorbed CO to form the electron enrichment area, providing the binding site for electrophile species (H+) (Figure S15).
The possible mechanism of CO2 reduction to CH4, C2H4 and HCOOH are
illustrated in Scheme S1.[59, 60] Before the state of CO*, COOH* or HCOO* is formed by the first proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) to CO2 (Scheme S1).[6,61] At the equilibrium potential under standard conditions (U = 0 V), some steps of CH4, C2H4 and HCOOH generating processes are uphill/endothermic (Figures 5a and S17), indicating that CO2 reduction reaction is unfavorable thermodynamically

and an external driving force (for example, electrical potential) is necessary. The CH4 pathways share two proton and electron transfer steps of protonation on CO* to form CHO* (Step 3) and further protonation at C to form CH2O* (Step 4). The following steps for CH4 Pathway 1 keep the protonation on C atom to form CH3O* and to generate CH4 in Step 6. After that, O* is hydrogenated to OH* and then to H2O. Alternatively, CH2OH* is formed in Step 9 of CH4 Pathway 2, then CH4 is released at the end. For CH4 Pathways 1 and 2, Step 1 from CO2 to COOH* shows the largest barrier, becoming the potential-determining step.[62] For CO* generation, the external applied potential requirement is at least -1.28 V vs. RHE to start the reaction on the Cu-Pd heterostructure (experimental electrolyte pH = 6.8). But the formation of HCOO* by the first PCET reaction to CO2 (Step 33) is downhill/exothermic for CH4 Pathways 3 and 4 (Figure 5a), which might be the first step for CH4 generation. In addition, HCOO* is the key intermediate for generating HCOOH, resulting in a certain amount of HCOOH component in the products (Figure 3). Similarly, thermodynamic feasibility of CO2 reduction to C2H4 from two bound CO* intermediates reveals that both C2H4 Pathway 1 and 2 show positive ΔG values for generating CHO*CO* (Step 16) and COHCO* (Step 25) (Figure 5a and Scheme S1). These results indicate that either the protonation at C atom of one CO* (Step 16) or C-C bonding coupled with protonation at O atom (Step 25) also needs extra energy to trigger. Moreover, the higher barriers of the potential-determining steps for C2H4 generation (Step 24 in Pathway 1 and Step 30 in Pathway 2) suggest that CO2 reduction to C2H4 on Cu-Pd heterostructure requires higher driving force compared Jo ur na l P re -p ro of
with the CH4 formation, indicating CH4 generation is more favorable on the Cu-Pd heterostructure.
To further reflect the practical conditions, pH, one of the important factors in the
selectivity of PCET reactions, including the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction in water, should be considered in the calculations.[63, 64] According to the correction in the model of the computational hydrogen electrode, the external applied potential requirement (-0.87 V vs. RHE) used to drive the CO2 conversion to CH4 under the experimental conditions (pH = 6.8, p = 1 bar, T = 298.15 K) could be determined. The detailed calculation description is shown in Supporting Information. As shown in Figure 5b, once the potential of -0.87 V vs. RHE was applied, the free energy profiles of the optimal CH4 formation pathway on the Cu-Pd heterostructure become downhill/exothermic but a few steps (Step 24 (CH2 *CH2 *(E9) → * + C2H4), Step 25 (CO*CO*(E1) + H+ + e-→ COHCO*(E10)), and Step 30 (CH2CHO *(E14) + H+ + e-→ O*(E15) + C2H4)) for C2H4 generation are still uphill/endothermic. Among them, Step 24 for C2H4 formation via C-C coupling of two CH2* is not a PCET reaction, so it could not be driven by the external electrical potential. For the C2H4 Pathway 2, the external applied potential requirement is at least -2.45 V vs. RHE to start the reaction (Figure S16), which is much higher than that for CH4 pathways. Thus, the theoretical calculations clearly suggest that the Cu-Pd heterostructure shows higher activity for CH4 production, which is consistent well with electrochemical measurement results.

Moreover, the difference of the external applied potential for driving the CH4 and C2H4 generation on Cu (111) is smaller than that on the Cu-Pd heterostructure (Figure 5 and S17). This might explain the experimental results that the pure Cu catalyst exhibited a lower yield of CH4. The results further suggest appropriate Pd composition plays a prominent role in directed-catalysis for CO2 reduction to the target product. Thus, the high activity and selectivity for CO2 reduction to CH4 on Cu-Pd heterostructure are confirmed at the molecular level, guaranteeing that CH4 is the dominate product in CO2 reduction on the Cu-based catalysts with optimized Pd contents. There are some CuPd bimetal catalysts with phase-separated configurations that favored C2H4 formation, while also some favored CH4 formation, this inconsistent selectivity between CH4 and C2H4 might be owing to the other structure factors apart from the configurations of Cu and Pd atoms in CuPd bimetal catalysts, such as size and exposed facet.[22, 65-69]

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In conclusion, the facile electroreduction of heterostructured CuCl-PdOx hexagonal microplates could result in Cu-Pd heterostructure. The obtained Cu-Pd heterostructure exhibited distinguished electrochemical CO2 reduction activity, with almost exclusive CH4 production capability compared to C2H4 and CO. Such an excellent selectivity on CH4 over C2H4 is of great importance for practical implementation. Tafel analysis

suggests that the presence of Cu-Pd interface could promote the reaction kinetics and enhance the selectivity of CO2 reduction. The DFT calculations further provide a molecular-level evidence that the Cu-Pd heterostructure shows a much lower demand of the extra energy for triggering CO2 reduction to form CH4 than C2H4. Therefore, the introduction of heterostructure as well as its facile synthesis provides a new strategy in the catalyst design for the electrochemical CO2 reduction, and opportunities of further unveiling the chemistry of this artificial carbon conversion reaction.
